source.title: Will Scaling Improve Social Simulation with LLMs?
source.authors: Caleb Ziems; William B. Held; Şura Karaca; David Grusky; Tatsunori B. Hashimoto; Di-Yi Yang

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to social-simulation tasks and examines whether their task loss and downstream accuracy improve with scale.
record.gate_note: The study measures social-task loss, not held-out language-model pretraining loss, so those results do not test V1. It discusses extrapolations from fitted curves but does not validate predictions against runs orders of magnitude larger. It selects compute-optimal token counts for each compute budget but does not report parameter/token allocation trends. General-benchmark correlations and loss-to-accuracy calibration results are included because they bear on downstream predictability. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits compute scaling laws for task loss on three social-simulation downstream tasks, using an IsoFLOP suite of 85 models. It also calibrates loss to accuracy across 35 open models and tests parameter scaling after fine-tuning. These results bear on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, validate extrapolations, report allocation exponents, vary architecture, or compare fitting choices.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that even fine-tuned Qwen2.5 and Llama3 models (0.5B–8B) show no parameter scaling on the null-scaling behavioural tasks. They conclude that scale alone is insufficient where human heuristics differ from those of models.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses controlled IsoFLOP sweeps for social-task loss and observational calibration across model families; it does not reproduce the original language-model pretraining-loss scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Observed scaling and calibration strength vary by task and population. The study notes that operationalization, prompt formatting, and metric choice can matter, but does not report a controlled comparison of those choices.

fits_no_version.finding: How strongly a WVS region's observational fit holds correlates with that region's term frequency in DCLM (Spearman 0.83, Pearson 0.73).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling gains on downstream tasks depend on how well the target domain is represented in pretraining data.

record.problems: The compute-scaling suite covers only 10^18 to 10^20 FLOPs, and the larger-scale utility estimates extrapolate beyond the fitted range without validation on larger runs. Several task-level fits are weak or non-significant. The reported fine-tuning nulls and significant comparisons are described in text, while their detailed values are shown in a figure.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports many additional per-region WVS and per-subtask Psych-101 compute fits and observational correlations in Figures 10–11, Figure 5, and Appendix Table 1. These were not all extracted individually; representative strong fits and the explicit null/non-significant cases were retained to capture task-dependent outcomes. Fine-tuning chart values for individual checkpoints were not transcribed because the prose gives aggregate significance results.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining loss is not reported; only social-task loss is measured.
Extrapolations beyond 1e20 FLOPs are forecasts and are never validated against larger runs.
The IsoFLOP optimum is used to select runs, but no trends in optimal parameter or token allocation are reported.
No other modalities are studied. Fine-tuning results report accuracy at a few model sizes, not a fitted power law.
No comparison of parameter counting, schedules, data or fitting methods. Variation across tasks is not variation from fitting choices.

missing.what: Four more Psych-101 subtasks have non-significant compute-scaling fits: Plonsky (slope -0.07), Somerville (-0.07), Bahrami (-0.08) and Waltz (-0.07). These are nulls bearing on V6, but only Schulz and Sadeghiyeh are recorded.
The authors' extrapolations for Gershman (about 40x compute to reach 90% accuracy) and Myanmar (83x) are forecasts. If kept at all, they should be marked as unvalidated.

record.verdict_notes: Social-task loss in this study is a downstream metric, so the compute-scaling rows belong under V6 rather than V1 or V7. Compute range is only two orders of magnitude (1e18–1e20). Fine-tuning used about 16M tokens per run.

versions.untested_parts: The reported loss is loss on social-simulation tasks, not held-out pretraining loss of language models.
Extrapolations are forecasts; the study does not compare them with runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitted runs.
Although compute-optimal token counts are selected at each budget, the study does not report how optimal parameter and token counts grow with compute.
The controlled suite fixes architecture; no comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count is reported.
The study concerns text-pretrained language models and does not test other modalities or the listed training regimes as a general scaling claim.
Tests social-simulation tasks and selected downstream accuracy calibrations; does not establish predictability for downstream tasks generally.
Reports variation across simulation tasks and populations, but does not compare alternative parameter-counting rules, fitting methods, or compute-optimal allocation laws.

relationships.condition: Aggregate WVS, Psych-101 and ACL task loss versus compute, and strong-scaling subtasks and regions
relationships.reason: Log-linear task-loss fits with r2 0.85–0.97 (R1–R3, R6, R7). Loss predicts accuracy in 16 of 17 WVS regions and linearly for ACL (R8, R10). PC1 explains 60% of loss variance for Canada and ACL (R11, R16). Fine-tuned models scale on Sadeghiyeh and the control tasks (R18, R20).
relationships.display_finding: Log-linear task-loss fits achieve R²=0.85–0.97, loss predicts accuracy in 16 of 17 WVS regions and linearly for ACL, and the first principal component explains 60% of loss variance for Canada and ACL; fine-tuned models also improve with scale on Sadeghiyeh and control tasks.
